name: Shower filter

lead: A shower filter attaches at the shower arm, as an inline unit or a showerhead with built-in media, to reduce chlorine in shower water. People buy them hoping for softer skin and hair, since retailers link chlorinated or hard water to dry skin and brittle hair.

Water passes through media such as KDF, calcium sulfite and activated carbon that react with or adsorb chlorine before leaving the showerhead. Certified models are tested under the NSF/ANSI 177 standard for free available chlorine. Descriptions call the evidence for skin and hair benefits limited and largely anecdotal, and no trials on skin or hair appearance were found.

paras: People screw the filter onto the shower arm or swap in a filtered showerhead and use it with their normal routine. Cartridges are replaced periodically, as the maker specifies. Users who report softer skin or hair describe it over days to weeks.

A 2022 hospital study reported that hollow-fibre shower filters did not prevent patient exposure to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and bacterial contamination of one filter type has been documented. Cartridges are described as needing periodic replacement.

angle.text: Shower filters reduce chlorine in the water, which retailers link to dry skin and brittle hair, so people use them hoping for softer skin and hair. The reported benefits are anecdotal, and no trials on skin or hair appearance were found.

lead: A shower filter is a point-of-use water filter fitted at the shower arm, either as an inline unit or as a showerhead with built-in media, intended to reduce contaminants in shower water, chiefly chlorine.[1] Retail marketing frames them as a way to ease dry skin and brittle hair attributed to chlorinated or hard water.

Descriptions say certified models are tested under the NSF/ANSI 177 standard for free available chlorine, and typically use media such as KDF, calcium sulfite and activated carbon.[1] The same description states that scientific evidence for skin and hair benefits is limited and largely anecdotal.[1]
No clinical trials of shower filters for skin or hair appearance were found. Hospital research has examined shower filters for a different purpose, bacterial exposure.[2]

paras: Inline filters sit between the shower arm and an existing showerhead, preserving the user's chosen head, while replacement showerheads integrate the media into one unit.[1] Filters do not usually address water hardness as such; descriptions say effects on hardness, metals and disinfection byproducts vary by model.[1]
Separately, calcium and magnesium deposits from hard water can clog showerheads and change spray patterns.[3]

Marketing and descriptions say reducing chlorine may mean less drying of skin and hair and less inhalation of chlorine vapor in hot showers, though these descriptions state that evidence is limited and the link to respiratory effects at municipal chlorine levels is not robust.[1]

A 2022 hospital study examined hollow-fibre shower filter heads and reported that they failed to prevent patient exposure to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, citing retrograde colonization of the filter mechanism.[2] The study concerned high-risk hospital patients, not cosmetic use.
No studies found on appearance outcomes. A hospital infection-control study of shower filters examined bacterial exposure rather than skin or hair.[2]
